cl_can_smoked_cancer.q: Does smoking cannabis cause lung cancer?
cl_can_smoked_cancer.short: Nobody knows yet. Pooled studies found no clear link; a Swedish study found about twice the rate in men who'd used cannabis over 50 times, against men who never had.
cl_can_smoked_cancer.but: Nearly all of those men also smoked tobacco. So the two can't be pulled apart.
how: Six studies comparing 2,159 people with lung cancer and 2,985 without were pooled. Regular cannabis smoking made no clear difference, even in people who didn't smoke tobacco, but a higher risk couldn't be ruled out. We know this pooled study only from a 2017 expert report.

A Swedish study followed 49,321 men for 40 years, from military call-up at 18 to 20 to about age 60. Men who said at call-up they'd used cannabis over 50 times got lung cancer about twice as often as men who said never. That held even allowing for the tobacco they smoked then.

But 91 in 100 of those men also smoked tobacco. The 678 men who used cannabis without tobacco had one lung cancer between them: too few to study cannabis alone. Below 50 uses, risk didn't clearly rise with more use, and nobody asked what anyone smoked later.

By about 60, 189 of the 49,321 men, about 4 in 1,000, had a lung cancer record; the paper doesn't say how many in each group. Lung cancer is usually found at about 70. An expert committee notes that cannabis smoke, like tobacco smoke, contains cancer-causing chemicals.
cl_can_smoked_cancer.rate: The pooled studies are known only second-hand. The Swedish study asked about cannabis once, at 18 to 20, and nearly all the men who used it most also smoked tobacco. The two point different ways.

cl_can_smoked_vs_vaped.q: Does vaped cannabis feel different from smoked?
cl_can_smoked_vs_vaped.short: It can. In one lab study, the same weed vaped felt stronger and raised heart rate more than smoked, but only at the lower of two amounts.
cl_can_smoked_vs_vaped.but: It's one study of 17 people who rarely use cannabis, with fixed amounts in a lab. Its authors say earlier studies found the two much alike.
how: 17 healthy adults came to a lab six times. On average, they hadn't used cannabis for about a year. Each time they got the same weed, smoked in a small pipe or breathed in from a vaporizer, at a lower or higher amount, or a dummy.

At the lower amount, heart rate rose by 23 beats a minute after vaping against 11 after smoking, and people rated the effect about 70 out of 100 against 46. At the higher amount, neither gap was clear. Blood THC ran higher after vaping, but the study didn't test whether that was more than chance.

Where the two ways differed on attention and speed tasks, all three gaps showed worse scores after vaping. At the higher amount, both raised bad feelings, anxiety, memory trouble and coughing, with no clear gap. Two people threw up (one after each way) and one hallucinated after vaping, all at the higher amount.

After the higher amount, people still rated an effect when their blood THC was back to zero. The study didn't test joints, bongs, handheld vapes, oil carts, concentrates, regular use, or effects on the lungs.
cl_can_smoked_vs_vaped.rate: One small lab study of 17 people who rarely use cannabis, at fixed amounts. People knew which way they were using, and with 32 things measured, a few gaps could show up by chance.

cl_can_vaped_lungs.q: Is vaping cannabis linked to breathing problems?
cl_can_vaped_lungs.short: In one survey, yes. About 1 in 4 who'd vaped cannabis in the past month reported a lasting cough, phlegm or bronchitis, against 1 in 8 who never had.
cl_can_vaped_lungs.but: It's what people said in one survey, with no lung tests, so it can't show cause. Even people who hadn't vaped cannabis for over 6 months reported more.
how: 2,553 young adults in Southern California, about 19 years old, answered once, in 2018 or 2019. The link held after allowing for nicotine vaping and for smoking cigarettes or cannabis. The 1 in 4 and 1 in 8 are our rough figures from the paper's counts; it gives no rates by group.

Wheezing was more common only in people who vaped cannabis on 3 or more days of the past month. Shortness of breath wasn't clearly more common. Nicotine vaping went with all three symptoms until cannabis vaping and smoking were counted, then with none.

The survey didn't ask what was vaped, how much, or whether tobacco went into joints. It ran until October 2019, during the US outbreak of lung injury from vaping (EVALI). So it can't say whether those products played a part.

A 2024 review found no study that compared people who vape cannabis with people who don't use it, or followed them over time. Its few vaping studies compared vaping with smoking, and none used oil carts or dabs. Vaping left less carbon monoxide in the breath than smoking, and in one study with no comparison group, symptoms eased after switching.
cl_can_vaped_lungs.rate: One survey that asked once about symptoms people reported, with no lung tests. People who hadn't vaped cannabis for months also reported more symptoms, so other differences may explain part of the link.

cl_can_evali.q: What was the 2019 vaping lung injury (EVALI)?
cl_can_evali.short: A US outbreak of serious lung injury in people who vaped. By January 2020, 2,668 had been in hospital, and most said they'd vaped THC.
cl_can_evali.but: The studies point to an additive, vitamin E acetate, but none tested whether it causes the injury. Other chemicals aren't ruled out.
how: To count, a person had vaped or dabbed in the past 90 days, had changes in the lungs on a scan, and had no other likely cause. Half were 24 or younger, and 66 in 100 were male. CDC figures quoted second-hand: 52 deaths by mid-December 2019, about 2 in 100 cases, and in an earlier count 47 in 100 needed intensive care.

Of 2,022 patients who said what they'd vaped in the 3 months before, 82 in 100 named a THC product and 14 in 100 only nicotine. Nobody checked their devices, and in one study THC turned up in the lungs of 9 of 11 patients who said they hadn't used it.

Vitamin E acetate, an oil sold online to thicken cannabis oil, was in lung fluid from 48 of 51 patients and none of 99 healthy people, who didn't vape THC. It was in 23 of 36 cartridge liquids from 10 New York patients. The papers call those cartridges illegal or fake, without saying how they knew.

None of this proves it caused the injury: the healthy people didn't vape THC, and nobody tested people who vaped the same products and stayed well, or what breathing it in does. The CDC says other chemicals aren't ruled out. Weed smoked, eaten or vaped as dried flower wasn't studied.
cl_can_evali.rate: Patients' own accounts of what they vaped, and lab tests of their lungs and cartridges. The healthy people compared hadn't vaped THC, and no study tested whether the additive causes the injury.

cl_can_edibles.q: What goes wrong with edibles, compared with smoking?
cl_can_edibles.short: At one US hospital, ER visits after edibles more often meant being too high, sudden mental-health symptoms or heart symptoms. Smoking or vaping visits more often meant vomiting.
cl_can_edibles.but: These are shares of hospital visits, not risks: nobody counted how many people used each form, or how much they took.
how: Of 2,567 ER visits judged partly due to cannabis at one Colorado hospital, 2012 to 2016, 238 (about 1 in 11) were linked to edibles. Being too high: 48 in 100 edible visits against 28 in 100 smoking or vaping visits; sudden mental-health symptoms, 18 against 11; heart symptoms, 8 against 3.

Edible visits less often involved stomach trouble or vomiting (15 in 100 against 32) or ended in a hospital stay (19 against 33). Because edibles were so few, most visits for being too high (647 of 762) still followed smoking or vaping. None of the 2,567 visits ended in death.

Two papers say eating acts later and lasts longer than inhaling, citing lab work; nobody timed it in these patients. A review says the delay may lead people to take more than they meant, and retells reports of people eating a whole edible after a first piece did nothing. In one case report, a 19-year-old in Colorado who did this in 2014 died, and the autopsy named cannabis intoxication a main factor.

The groups differed: edible visits more often came from women (51 in 100 against 33) and from people living outside Colorado (41 against 7). Nobody tested the products. None of these sources studied the lungs of adults who eat cannabis.
cl_can_edibles.rate: One hospital's records, with no count of how many people used each form or how much they took, and no allowance for how the groups differed. What's said about the slow start comes from papers citing lab work.

cl_can_edibles_labels.q: Do edible labels show how much THC is inside?
cl_can_edibles_labels.short: Mostly not, in a 2014 US test: 17 in 100 edibles matched their THC label, 23 in 100 held more, and 60 in 100 held less.
cl_can_edibles_labels.but: It's one test of 75 edibles from three US cities, not picked at random. Rules and products may differ elsewhere and now.
how: 75 edibles of 47 brands (baked goods, drinks, candy and chocolate) were bought at nine medical-cannabis shops in San Francisco, Los Angeles and Seattle in 2014. A lab measured the THC in each whole package; within a tenth of the label counted as a match.

Those with less THC than labelled held about half the labelled amount on average, and some had almost none. Those with more held about 28% more on average. Seattle had the most with less (18 of 23), and Los Angeles the most with more (9 of 20).

Only 13 products printed their CBD, and none was within a tenth of it, though 44 of the 75 had some CBD. Each package was mixed before testing, so the test can't say how evenly THC was spread between pieces.

No effects on people were measured: the authors' warnings about too little or too much THC are their own reasoning. Werc Shop Laboratories, which four of the six authors are linked to, paid for the lab tests.
cl_can_edibles_labels.rate: One lab test of 75 products from three US cities in 2014, not chosen at random. It measured what was inside, not effects on people, and can't speak for other places or later years.

cannabis.statement: Research has shown that smoking weed doesn't raise lung cancer risk.
cannabis.why: Pooled studies found no clear link, but a higher risk couldn't be ruled out. A Swedish study found about twice the rate in men who'd used cannabis over 50 times, though nearly all of them also smoked tobacco.

cannabis.statement: Once THC is gone from your blood, the effects are over.
cannabis.why: In one lab study of 17 people, after the higher amount, people still rated an effect when their blood THC was back to zero.

cannabis.statement: Young adults who vape weed report more cough and phlegm than those who never have.
cannabis.why: In one survey, about 1 in 4 who'd vaped cannabis in the past month reported a lasting cough, phlegm or bronchitis, against 1 in 8 who never had. It's what people said, so it can't show cause.

cannabis.statement: Most people hurt in the 2019 vaping lung outbreak said they had vaped THC.
cannabis.why: Of 2,022 US patients who said what they'd vaped, 82 in 100 named a THC product and 14 in 100 only nicotine. Nobody checked their devices.

cannabis.statement: Vitamin E acetate has been proven to cause the 2019 vaping lung injuries.
cannabis.why: It was in lung fluid from 48 of 51 patients and none of 99 healthy people, but no study tested whether it causes the injury, and other chemicals aren't ruled out.

cannabis.statement: Most ER visits for being too high on weed follow edibles.
cannabis.why: At one Colorado hospital, 647 of 762 such visits followed smoking or vaping, and edibles were about 1 in 11 of all its cannabis visits. These are shares of visits, not risks.

cannabis.statement: ER visits after edibles involve heart symptoms more often than visits after smoking or vaping.
cannabis.why: At one US hospital, heart symptoms came up in 8 in 100 edible visits, against 3 in 100 smoking or vaping visits. Nobody counted how much people had taken.

cannabis.statement: The THC number on an edible's label is usually right.
cannabis.why: In a 2014 test of 75 US edibles, only 17 in 100 were within a tenth of their label; 60 in 100 held less and 23 in 100 more. It's one test, not picked at random.
